Thomas Edison.bio: Thomas Edison was an American inventor who developed the phonograph, the motion picture camera and the first practical electric light bulb. He held over a thousand US patents and founded the first industrial research laboratory at Menlo Park, New Jersey.

Yogi Berra.bio: Yogi Berra was an American professional baseball catcher who played nineteen seasons with the New York Yankees, winning ten World Series championships. He was almost equally famous for his paradoxical, humorous sayings — 'Yogi-isms' such as 'It ain't over till it's over'.

Johann Wolfgang von Goethe.bio: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe was a German writer, poet, playwright and natural philosopher, regarded as Germany's greatest literary figure. His works include the drama Faust, The Sorrows of Young Werther and Wilhelm Meister's Apprenticeship.

Carl Sandburg.bio: American poet, journalist and historian. He won three Pulitzer Prizes, two for poetry collections such as Chicago Poems and one for his biography of Abraham Lincoln.

Margaret Sangster.bio: Margaret E. Sangster was an American poet, author and editor who edited Harper's Bazaar from 1889 to 1899 and wrote popular books and verses for young women, including 'Winsome Womanhood' (1900).

Iris Murdoch.bio: Dame Iris Murdoch was an Irish-British novelist and philosopher whose works, including The Sea, The Sea and Under the Net, explore good and evil, morality and the inner life. She won the Booker Prize in 1978.

Wayne Dyer.bio: Wayne Dyer was an American self-help author and motivational speaker whose first book, Your Erroneous Zones (1976), became one of the best-selling books of all time. He wrote more than forty books and lectured widely on self-development and spirituality.

Henry J. Kaiser.bio: Henry J. Kaiser was an American industrialist whose shipyards built Liberty ships at record speed during World War II. His companies also produced steel, aluminum and automobiles, and he founded the Kaiser Permanente health system.

Publilius Syrus.bio: Publilius Syrus was a Latin writer of the 1st century BC who was brought to Italy as a slave from Syria and later freed. He is known for his Sententiae, a collection of moral maxims drawn from his mimes.

Napoleon Hill.bio: Napoleon Hill was an American self-help author best known for Think and Grow Rich (1937), one of the best-selling books of its kind. His work popularized the idea that success follows from definite purpose and a positive mental attitude.

Donald Trump.bio: Donald Trump is an American businessman and television personality who served as the 45th President of the United States (2017–2021) and was elected again as the 47th President in 2024. Before politics he built a real-estate business and hosted the reality show The Apprentice.

Benjamin Spock.bio: American pediatrician whose The Common Sense Book of Baby and Child Care (1946) transformed child-rearing advice and became one of the best-selling books of the 20th century.

Sigmund Freud.bio: Sigmund Freud was an Austrian neurologist who founded psychoanalysis, developing concepts such as the unconscious, the Oedipus complex and talk therapy. His theories profoundly influenced psychology, literature and 20th-century culture, though many are now scientifically disputed.

Christopher Reeve.bio: Christopher Reeve was an American actor best known for playing Superman in the 1978 film and its sequels. After a 1995 horse-riding accident left him paralysed, he became a prominent advocate for spinal-cord research.

Albert Einstein.bio: German-born theoretical physicist who developed the theory of relativity, one of the pillars of modern physics. He won the 1921 Nobel Prize in Physics for his explanation of the photoelectric effect.

Charles Kettering.bio: Charles F. Kettering, American inventor and head of research at General Motors for nearly three decades. He invented the electric self-starter for automobiles and founded the Delco electronics company.

V. Naipaul.bio: V. S. Naipaul was a Trinidadian-British novelist known for works such as A House for Mr Biswas and In a Free State, which won the Booker Prize. He received the Nobel Prize in Literature in 2001 and was knighted in 1990.

John Wooden.bio: John Wooden was the head coach of UCLA men's basketball, winning ten NCAA championships in twelve years, including seven in a row. His 'Pyramid of Success' and teachings on character made him one of the most quoted figures in coaching.

Haddon Robinson.bio: Haddon W. Robinson was an American evangelical preacher and professor of preaching, and a longtime president of Gordon-Conwell Theological Seminary. His book Biblical Preaching is a standard text on expository preaching.

Pearl Buck.bio: Pearl S. Buck was an American writer who spent much of her early life in China, where her parents were missionaries. Her novel The Good Earth won the Pulitzer Prize, and she received the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1938.

Brian Tracy.bio: Canadian-American motivational speaker and self-development author. His books, including Eat That Frog! and The Psychology of Achievement, focus on goals, time management and sales success.

Larry Elder.bio: Larry Elder is an American conservative talk radio host and author, known as the 'Sage from South Central' for his long-running syndicated Los Angeles radio show. His books include 'The Ten Things You Can't Say in America' (2000).

Michael Korda.bio: Michael Korda is an English-born writer and editor who served as editor-in-chief of Simon & Schuster. He has written bestselling biographies, memoirs and novels, including works on T. E. Lawrence and Dwight D. Eisenhower.

James Russell Lowell.bio: James Russell Lowell was an American Romantic poet, critic, editor and diplomat, one of the Fireside Poets. He was the first editor of The Atlantic Monthly and later served as U.S. minister to Spain and Britain.

Yoda.bio: Yoda is a fictional Jedi Master in the Star Wars films, the wise, centuries-old teacher of Luke Skywalker. His distinctive inverted speech and sayings about the Force have made him one of cinema's most quoted characters.

Harriet Beecher Stowe.bio: Harriet Beecher Stowe was an American author and abolitionist whose novel Uncle Tom's Cabin (1852) galvanized anti-slavery sentiment in the United States and abroad. She wrote more than 30 books, including novels, travel memoirs and collections of articles.

Murray Gell-Mann.bio: Murray Gell-Mann was an American physicist who proposed the quark model of particle physics and won the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1969. He later co-founded the Santa Fe Institute to study complex systems.

Pericles.bio: Pericles was an influential Athenian statesman and general during Athens' Golden Age in the 5th century BC. Under his leadership Athens built the Parthenon and developed its democratic institutions; he died during the Peloponnesian War.

Baltasar Gracian.bio: Spanish Jesuit and baroque prose writer. His The Art of Worldly Wisdom (1647), a collection of 300 maxims on prudence and success, has influenced readers from Schopenhauer to modern executives.

Cullen Hightower.bio: Cullen Hightower was an American humorist and aphorist whose one-line observations on business and human nature were widely syndicated in newspapers.

African proverb.bio: An attribution used for traditional sayings from African oral traditions, passed down through generations rather than written by a single known author.

Bodhidharma.bio: Buddhist monk of the 5th or 6th century, traditionally credited with bringing Chan Buddhism to China, where it later developed into Zen in Japan. Legend also links him to the Shaolin Monastery and the origins of Shaolin martial arts.

Princess Diana.bio: Diana, Princess of Wales, was a member of the British royal family as the first wife of Charles, Prince of Wales (later King Charles III). She was known worldwide for her charity work, particularly on landmines and HIV/AIDS, and died in a car crash in Paris.

John Pierrakos.bio: John C. Pierrakos was a Greek-American psychiatrist who co-founded Bioenergetic Analysis with Alexander Lowen and later founded Core Energetics, a body-centred approach to psychotherapy and personal growth. He authored 'Core Energetics' (1990) and 'Eros, Love and Sexuality'.

Richard Bach.bio: Richard Bach is an American writer best known for the bestselling novella Jonathan Livingston Seagull (1970) and Illusions (1977). A former Air Force pilot, his work often combines flying with spiritual themes.

Napoleon Bonaparte.bio: Napoleon Bonaparte was a French military leader who rose to prominence during the French Revolution and became Emperor of the French in 1804. His Napoleonic Wars reshaped Europe, and his Napoleonic Code influenced legal systems worldwide. He died in exile on Saint Helena.

Bo Jackson.bio: Vincent Edward 'Bo' Jackson, American athlete who starred in both professional football and baseball. He remains the only athlete named an All-Star in two major American sports, in the NFL Pro Bowl and the MLB All-Star Game.

Liberace.bio: Liberace (Wladziu Valentino Liberace) was an American pianist and showman famous for his flamboyant costumes, candelabra-topped piano and lavish stage shows, which made him one of the highest-paid entertainers of the 1950s and 1960s.

William Arthur Ward.bio: William Arthur Ward was an American writer of inspirational maxims and short poems, famous for lines about gratitude, attitude and possibility. His epigrams appeared in newspapers and magazines for decades and are widely quoted in motivational literature.

Ellen Gilchrist.bio: Ellen Gilchrist was an American novelist and short-story writer whose fiction was set largely in the American South. Her collection Victory Over Japan won the National Book Award in 1984.

Carl Jung.bio: Swiss psychiatrist who founded analytical psychology. His concepts of the collective unconscious, archetypes and introversion and extraversion remain influential in psychology and culture.

Lord Herbert.bio: Edward Herbert, 1st Baron Herbert of Cherbury, was an English soldier, diplomat, poet and philosopher, often called the father of English deism for his work 'De Veritate' (1624).

Anne Wilson Schaef.bio: American psychotherapist and author known for When Society Becomes an Addict (1987) and Women's Reality. She developed her own therapeutic approach after years working in addiction treatment.

Elizabeth Browning.bio: Elizabeth Barrett Browning was an English poet of the Victorian era, famed for Sonnets from the Portuguese and the verse-novel Aurora Leigh. She was among the most prominent British poets of her time.

German proverb.bio: A traditional German proverb, passed down through generations of folk wisdom.

Germaine de Stael.bio: Germaine de Staël, known as Madame de Staël, was a Swiss-French writer and political thinker whose works, including 'Corinne' (1807) and 'De l'Allemagne' (1810), shaped European Romanticism. A prominent critic of Napoleon, she spent years in exile from France.

Bernadette Devlin.bio: Irish socialist and republican activist, now known as Bernadette McAliskey. Elected to the British Parliament in 1969 at the age of 21, she was then its youngest member and a prominent voice of the Northern Ireland civil rights movement.

American proverb.bio: An attribution used for traditional sayings of American folk origin, passed down through generations rather than written by a single known author.

Jon Kabat-Zinn.bio: Jon Kabat-Zinn is an American professor emeritus of medicine who founded the Stress Reduction Clinic at the University of Massachusetts in 1979 and developed Mindfulness-Based Stress Reduction (MBSR). His books include 'Full Catastrophe Living' and 'Wherever You Go, There You Are'.

Theophrastus.bio: Theophrastus was a Greek philosopher who succeeded Aristotle as head of the Lyceum in Athens. Known as the father of botany for his works on plants, he also wrote Characters, a set of sketches of moral types that influenced later literature.

Tony Robbins.bio: Tony Robbins is an American author, coach and motivational speaker known for bestselling books such as Unlimited Power and Awaken the Giant Within. His seminars and self-help programmes have made him one of the most prominent figures in the personal development industry.

Gloria Steinem.bio: Gloria Steinem is an American journalist and social-political activist who became a leading voice of the feminist movement in the late 1960s and 1970s. She co-founded Ms. magazine in 1972.

Mary McLeod Bethune.bio: Mary McLeod Bethune was an American educator and civil rights leader who founded a school for girls in Daytona Beach, Florida, that became Bethune-Cookman University. She advised President Franklin D. Roosevelt and founded the National Council of Negro Women in 1935.

Voltaire.bio: Voltaire, born François-Marie Arouet, was a French Enlightenment writer, philosopher and historian famous for the novella Candide and for his witty defence of civil liberties, including freedom of speech and religion. He was one of the most prolific and influential writers of his age.

Joseph Stalin.bio: Joseph Stalin ruled the Soviet Union from the mid-1920s until his death in 1953, overseeing forced industrialisation and collectivisation, the Great Terror, and the Soviet war effort against Nazi Germany in the Second World War.

Thomas Fuller.bio: Thomas Fuller was an English physician and clergyman best known for Gnomologia (1732), a vast collection of proverbs and aphorisms, many of them his own. His concise moral sayings remain a staple of quotation collections.

Elbert Hubbard.bio: Elbert Hubbard was an American writer, publisher and philosopher who founded the Roycroft arts-and-crafts community. His essay "A Message to Garcia" (1899) was one of the most widely reprinted works of its era; he died in the sinking of the Lusitania.

Turkish proverb.bio: A traditional Turkish saying, passed down through generations as part of Turkey's folk wisdom.

Hugh Miller.bio: Hugh Miller was a Scottish stonemason, geologist and writer whose popular books, including The Old Red Sandstone, brought geology to a wide Victorian readership.

A. Powell Davies.bio: British-born American Unitarian clergyman who served as minister of All Souls Church in Washington, D.C. from 1944 until his death. A leading liberal preacher, he was known for defending civil liberties during the McCarthy era.

John Dryden.bio: John Dryden was an English poet, playwright and critic who dominated Restoration literature and became England's first Poet Laureate in 1668. His works include the satires Absalom and Achitophel and Mac Flecknoe.

Friedrich von Schiller.bio: Friedrich Schiller was a German poet, playwright and philosopher whose dramas include The Robbers, Wallenstein and Wilhelm Tell. His "Ode to Joy" was set to music by Beethoven in the Ninth Symphony.

Mike Ditka.bio: Mike Ditka is an American former football player and coach who played tight end in the NFL and coached the Chicago Bears to victory in Super Bowl XX. He is one of only two people to win an NFL championship as a player, assistant coach and head coach.

Jonathan Kozol.bio: Jonathan Kozol is an American writer and educator whose books expose inequality in public education, beginning with 'Death at an Early Age' (1967), drawn from his experience teaching in Boston schools. Later works include 'Savage Inequalities' (1991) and 'The Shame of the Nation' (2005).

Janis Joplin.bio: Janis Joplin was an American singer celebrated for her raw, powerful blues-rock voice in songs like 'Piece of My Heart' and 'Me and Bobby McGee.' She died at 27 and remains an icon of 1960s rock.

Honore de Balzac.bio: Honoré de Balzac was a French novelist and playwright whose vast sequence La Comédie humaine portrayed French society after Napoleon in more than 90 works. He is regarded as one of the founders of realism in literature.

Manuel Puig.bio: Manuel Puig was an Argentine novelist whose works, including 'Betrayed by Rita Hayworth' (1968) and 'Kiss of the Spider Woman' (1976), blend popular culture, cinema and experimental narrative.

William R. Inge.bio: William Ralph Inge was an English Anglican priest, professor and author who served as Dean of St Paul's Cathedral in London. Nicknamed 'the Gloomy Dean' for his pessimistic newspaper columns, he wrote widely on mysticism and Plotinus.

Jim Rohn.bio: Emanuel James Rohn, known as Jim Rohn, was an American entrepreneur and motivational speaker whose seminars and books on personal development influenced a generation of speakers, including Tony Robbins.

Saint Augustine.bio: Saint Augustine of Hippo was a North African theologian and philosopher whose writings shaped Western Christianity and philosophy. His works include Confessions, an early autobiography, and The City of God.

Maya Lin.bio: Maya Lin is an American designer and artist who, while still an undergraduate at Yale, won the national design competition for the Vietnam Veterans Memorial in Washington, D.C. She is known for works that blend art, architecture and landscape.

Jonas Salk.bio: Jonas Salk was an American physician and virologist who developed one of the first successful polio vaccines, announced in 1955. He later founded the Salk Institute for Biological Studies in California.

Peter Drucker.bio: Peter F. Drucker was an Austrian-American management consultant and writer widely regarded as the founder of modern management theory. His books, including The Practice of Management, shaped how organizations are run.

Luisa Sigea.bio: Luisa Sigea de Velasco was a Spanish-Portuguese Renaissance humanist and poet at the court of Lisbon, celebrated across Europe for her mastery of Latin, Greek, Hebrew and other languages. Her works include the Latin poem 'Syntra' (1546).

Jason Fried.bio: Jason Fried is an American entrepreneur, co-founder and CEO of the software company Basecamp (formerly 37signals). He co-authored the business books Rework and Remote.

Babe Ruth.bio: George Herman 'Babe' Ruth, American baseball legend. His prodigious home-run hitting with the New York Yankees, 714 in his career, transformed baseball and made him a national icon.

Thomas Carlyle.bio: Thomas Carlyle was a Scottish historian, philosopher and essayist whose works, including Sartor Resartus and On Heroes, Hero-Worship, and the Heroic in History, shaped Victorian thought. His history of the French Revolution is regarded as a classic of the genre.

Leo Buscaglia.bio: Leo Buscaglia was an American author and motivational speaker and a professor at the University of Southern California, whose popular course on 'Love' led to bestselling books including 'Love' (1972) and 'Living, Loving and Learning' (1982).

Indira Gandhi.bio: Indira Gandhi was the first and only woman prime minister of India, serving 1966–1977 and again from 1980 until her assassination in 1984. The daughter of Jawaharlal Nehru, she led India through war, the Green Revolution and the controversial Emergency.

Willa Cather.bio: Willa Cather was an American novelist known for her portrayals of frontier life on the Great Plains, including O Pioneers!, My Ántonia and Death Comes for the Archbishop. She won the Pulitzer Prize for Fiction in 1923 for One of Ours.

Jean de la Fontaine.bio: Jean de La Fontaine was a French poet famous for his Fables, collections of short moral tales in verse retold from Aesop and other sources. They remain classics of French literature, read by generations of French schoolchildren.

Thomas Jefferson.bio: Thomas Jefferson was an American statesman and Founding Father who wrote the Declaration of Independence and served as the third President of the United States (1801–1809). He founded the University of Virginia and doubled the nation's size with the Louisiana Purchase.

Thomas Dewar.bio: Thomas Dewar, later Baron Dewar, was a Scottish businessman who, with his brother John, built Dewar's whisky into a global brand. A celebrated traveller and wit, he was famous for his aphorisms, known as 'Dewarisms'.

George Patton.bio: George S. Patton Jr. was a senior officer of the United States Army who commanded the Seventh Army in the Mediterranean and the Third Army in France and Germany after D-Day in World War II. He was renowned for his aggressive leadership and flamboyant style.

Benjamin Disraeli.bio: British statesman who served twice as Prime Minister and led the Conservative Party. He was also a successful novelist, writing books such as Coningsby and Sybil.

Horace Friess.bio: Horace L. Friess was an American philosopher who taught at Columbia University for four decades. He wrote on religion, ethics and the philosophy of Felix Adler, founder of the Ethical Culture movement.

Haynes Bayly.bio: Thomas Haynes Bayly was an English poet, novelist and songwriter whose ballads, including 'She Wore a Wreath of Roses,' were widely popular in the 19th century.

Lauren Bacall.bio: Lauren Bacall was an American actress known for her distinctive voice and roles in film noir classics including 'To Have and Have Not' (1944) and 'The Big Sleep' (1946), opposite Humphrey Bogart, whom she married. She later won two Tony Awards for her work on Broadway.

Frank Herbert.bio: Frank Herbert was an American science-fiction author best known for Dune (1965), the best-selling science-fiction novel of all time, and its sequels. The series explored ecology, politics, religion and power.

J. Willard Marriott.bio: John Willard Marriott was an American entrepreneur who built a root beer stand into the Marriott hotel and food-services empire. A devout Latter-day Saint, he founded one of the world's largest hospitality companies.

Edward Gibbon.bio: Edward Gibbon was an English historian whose six-volume History of the Decline and Fall of the Roman Empire (1776–1789) remains a landmark of historical writing.

Og Mandino.bio: Og Mandino was an American author and sales mentor best known for The Greatest Salesman in the World (1968), a bestselling parable of success principles told through scrolls.

Lewis B. Smedes.bio: Lewis B. Smedes was a Dutch-American Christian theologian and ethicist who taught at Fuller Theological Seminary. His influential books include 'Forgive and Forget' (1984), on the healing power of forgiveness.

Laurence J. Peter.bio: Laurence J. Peter was a Canadian educator who formulated the 'Peter Principle' - the idea that employees in a hierarchy rise to their level of incompetence - in the bestselling satirical book 'The Peter Principle' (1969), written with Raymond Hull.

Hannah More.bio: Hannah More was an English writer, philanthropist and social reformer, and a member of the Bluestocking circle. She wrote influential tracts, campaigned against the slave trade, and founded schools for the poor.

William Yeats.bio: William Butler Yeats was an Irish poet and playwright, a driving force of the Irish Literary Revival and co-founder of the Abbey Theatre. He received the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1923, and poems such as 'The Second Coming' and 'Sailing to Byzantium' rank among the most famous of the twentieth century.

Ken S. Keyes.bio: Ken Keyes Jr. was an American personal-growth author best known for 'The Handbook to Higher Consciousness' (1973). Paralysed by polio as a young man, he founded a centre in Oregon teaching his 'Living Love' system for achieving happiness.

Kenneth Patton.bio: Kenneth L. Patton was an American Unitarian Universalist minister associated with Boston's Charles Street Meeting House, known for his humanist services, hymns and writings celebrating the natural world and the human spirit.

Eden Phillpotts.bio: Eden Phillpotts was an English novelist, poet and playwright best known for his novels set on Dartmoor, including Widecombe Fair.

Augustine of Hippo.bio: Saint Augustine of Hippo, one of the most influential thinkers in Western Christianity. His Confessions and The City of God shaped theology and philosophy for more than a thousand years.

Henri-Frederic Amiel.bio: Henri-Frédéric Amiel was a Swiss philosopher, poet and critic, and a professor at the University of Geneva. He is best known for his Journal Intime, a vast private diary published after his death.

Louisa Alcott.bio: Louisa May Alcott was an American novelist best known for 'Little Women' (1868), the semi-autobiographical story of the March sisters, which has remained in print ever since. She also wrote sensation fiction under a pen name and supported abolition and women's suffrage.

Annie Dillard.bio: American author whose Pilgrim at Tinker Creek (1974) won the Pulitzer Prize for General Nonfiction. Her prose is noted for its intense observation of the natural world and its spiritual questioning.

Man Ray.bio: Man Ray, born Emmanuel Radnitzky, was an American visual artist central to the Dada and Surrealist movements in Paris. He is known for his experimental 'rayograph' photographs and his portraits of leading artists and writers.

Henry Ford.bio: Henry Ford was an American industrialist who founded the Ford Motor Company and revolutionized manufacturing with the moving assembly line. His Model T made the automobile affordable for ordinary families.

Lily Tomlin.bio: Lily Tomlin is an American actress and comedian who rose to fame on 'Rowan & Martin's Laugh-In' and went on to acclaimed work in films such as 'Nashville' (1975) and the series 'Grace and Frankie', winning Emmy, Grammy and Tony Awards.

Martin Fischer.bio: Martin H. Fischer was a German-American physician and professor of physiology at the University of Cincinnati, remembered for his witty aphorisms about science, medicine and education, which were widely quoted and collected after his death.

John Adams.bio: John Adams was an American statesman and Founding Father who served as the first vice president and second president of the United States (1797–1801). A leader of the independence movement, he died on 4 July 1826, the same day as Thomas Jefferson.

Calvin Coolidge.bio: John Calvin Coolidge, 30th President of the United States (1923-1929). Nicknamed 'Silent Cal' for his taciturn manner, he presided over the prosperity of the Roaring Twenties.

General Douglas MacArthur.bio: Douglas MacArthur was an American five-star general who commanded Allied forces in the Southwest Pacific during the Second World War and later led UN forces in the Korean War. He accepted Japan's surrender aboard the USS Missouri in 1945.

Julius Charles Hare.bio: Julius Charles Hare was an English cleric and writer, Archdeacon of Lewes, who co-authored 'Guesses at Truth' (1827) with his brother Augustus Hare and wrote widely on theology, literature and German philosophy.

Buckminster Fuller.bio: R. Buckminster Fuller, American architect, inventor and futurist. He popularised the geodesic dome and wrote Operating Manual for Spaceship Earth, urging efficient use of the planet's resources.

Walter Lippmann.bio: Walter Lippmann was an American writer, reporter and political commentator who won two Pulitzer Prizes. His book Public Opinion (1922) is a foundational work on media and democracy, and he helped popularise the term 'Cold War'.

Eckhart Tolle.bio: Eckhart Tolle is a German-born spiritual teacher living in Canada, author of The Power of Now (1997) and A New Earth (2005), books on presence and the ego that became international bestsellers.

H. Jackson Browne.bio: H. Jackson Brown Jr. was an American author best known for Life's Little Instruction Book, a collection of advice written for his son that became a New York Times bestseller.

Marquis Vauvenargues.bio: Luc de Clapiers, Marquis de Vauvenargues, was a French moralist and aphorist whose 'Réflexions et maximes' (1746) is a classic of French moral literature, published shortly before his early death at thirty-one.

Charlotte Bronte.bio: Charlotte Brontë was an English novelist and poet, the eldest of the Brontë sisters. She is best known for Jane Eyre (1847), published under the pen name Currer Bell, a landmark of English literature.

Andy Warhol.bio: American artist and the leading figure of the pop art movement. His silkscreens of Campbell's Soup cans and Marilyn Monroe, and his prediction of fifteen minutes of fame, made him an icon of 20th-century art.

Pema Chodron.bio: Pema Chodron is an American nun in the Tibetan Buddhist tradition and a widely read author and teacher. Her books, including When Things Fall Apart, bring Buddhist teachings on compassion and difficulty to a broad audience.

Morris West.bio: Morris West was an Australian novelist whose works often explored the Catholic Church and moral dilemmas. His best-known novels include The Shoes of the Fisherman and The Devil's Advocate.

Franklin Roosevelt.bio: Franklin Delano Roosevelt was the 32nd President of the United States, the only president elected four times. He led the country through the Great Depression with the New Deal and through most of the Second World War.

Edwin Chapin.bio: Edwin Hubbell Chapin was an American Universalist minister and orator, among the most popular preachers and lecturers of his day.

Les Brown.bio: Les Brown is an American motivational speaker and former Ohio state legislator, known for his high-energy speeches and books including 'Live Your Dreams' (1992) and his catchphrase 'It's not over until you win'.

Havelock Ellis.bio: Henry Havelock Ellis was a British physician, writer and social reformer who pioneered the scientific study of human sexuality. His multi-volume Studies in the Psychology of Sex was groundbreaking and controversial in its time.

John Ruskin.bio: John Ruskin was the leading English art critic of the Victorian era, championing J.M.W. Turner and the Pre-Raphaelites in 'Modern Painters'. His later writings on society, work and education influenced reformers from William Morris to Gandhi.

Thomas Hardy.bio: Thomas Hardy was an English novelist and poet whose works, including Tess of the d'Urbervilles, Far from the Madding Crowd and Jude the Obscure, are set in the fictional county of Wessex. His writing is marked by a pessimistic view of fate and Victorian society.

Leon Blum.bio: Léon Blum was a French socialist politician who led the Popular Front government as prime minister in 1936-37 and served again briefly in 1938 and 1946-47. A literary critic as well as a statesman, he survived imprisonment under the Vichy regime and deportation by the Nazis.

Sam Keen.bio: Sam Keen is an American philosopher, professor and author known for Fire in the Belly (1991), a bestseller of the men's movement, and for writings that bring philosophy into everyday life.

John Astin.bio: John Astin is an American actor best known for playing Gomez Addams in the 1960s television series The Addams Family. He later taught acting and directing at Johns Hopkins University.

Henry Moore.bio: Henry Moore was an English sculptor best known for his monumental semi-abstract bronze figures, especially reclining figures and mother-and-child forms, set in landscapes around the world.

George Sheehan.bio: George A. Sheehan was an American cardiologist who took up running in his forties and became a leading voice of the running boom through his books and Runner's World columns.

Antoine de Saint-Exupery.bio: French writer and pioneering aviator, author of The Little Prince (1943), one of the most translated books ever published. He disappeared on a reconnaissance flight over the Mediterranean in 1944.

Marcel Proust.bio: Marcel Proust was a French novelist whose seven-volume 'In Search of Lost Time' ('À la recherche du temps perdu'), published between 1913 and 1927, is regarded as one of the greatest works of modern literature, exploring memory, time and art.

Louise Hay.bio: Louise Hay was an American motivational author whose 'You Can Heal Your Life' (1984) became a foundational text of the self-help movement. In 1987 she founded Hay House, which grew into a major publisher of self-help and spiritual books.

W. Clement Stone.bio: W. Clement Stone was an American businessman and philanthropist who built the Combined Insurance Company of America from a small agency into a major insurer. He co-authored success literature with Napoleon Hill, including Success Through a Positive Mental Attitude.

John Quincy Adams.bio: John Quincy Adams, son of President John Adams, was the sixth president of the United States (1825-1829) and one of its most accomplished diplomats. After his presidency he served nearly two decades in the House of Representatives, where he became a leading voice against slavery.

William Saroyan.bio: William Saroyan was an American novelist, playwright and short-story writer of Armenian descent, known for The Time of Your Life and the novel The Human Comedy. His warm stories of ordinary people in Fresno, California, won him the Pulitzer Prize for Drama, which he declined.

Isaac Asimov.bio: Isaac Asimov was an American writer and biochemistry professor, one of the most prolific authors of the 20th century. He is best known for the Foundation and Robot series and for his 'Three Laws of Robotics.'

Henry Van Dyke.bio: Henry van Dyke was an American author, educator and Presbyterian clergyman, and a professor of English literature at Princeton. He wrote the beloved Christmas story 'The Story of the Other Wise Man.'

Anthony Robbins.bio: American motivational speaker and life coach, better known as Tony Robbins. His books Unlimited Power (1986) and Awaken the Giant Within (1991) made him one of the most popular self-help figures in the world.

M. Scott Peck.bio: M. Scott Peck was an American psychiatrist whose book 'The Road Less Traveled' (1978) - opening with the line 'Life is difficult' - spent years on the bestseller lists and blended psychology with spirituality. He later wrote 'The Different Drum' and 'People of the Lie'.

Maureen Dowd.bio: Maureen Dowd is an American columnist for The New York Times, known for her sharp political commentary. She won the Pulitzer Prize for Commentary in 1999 for her coverage of the Clinton-Lewinsky scandal.

Christopher Morley.bio: Christopher Morley was an American journalist, novelist and poet, and a founder of the Saturday Review of Literature. He is known for novels such as Parnassus on Wheels and Kitty Foyle.

Hannah Arendt.bio: Hannah Arendt was a German-American political theorist whose works include The Origins of Totalitarianism and The Human Condition. She coined the phrase 'the banality of evil' in her report on the Eichmann trial.

Alan Cohen.bio: American inspirational author and speaker. His books, including A Deep Breath of Life, focus on spirituality, healing and personal growth.

Aldous Huxley.bio: English writer best known for the dystopian novel Brave New World (1932). He later explored mysticism and psychedelics in works such as The Doors of Perception (1954).

Marian Edelman.bio: Marian Wright Edelman is an American lawyer and activist who founded the Children's Defense Fund in 1973, becoming a leading national voice for poor and disadvantaged children. Her books include 'The Measure of Our Success' (1992).

Sue Patton Thoele.bio: Sue Patton Thoele is an American author of inspirational and self-help books, including The Courage to Be Yourself and The Mindful Woman. Her writing focuses on emotional strength, self-compassion and personal growth, especially for women.

Frank Crane.bio: Frank Crane was an American Presbyterian minister and syndicated newspaper columnist whose short essays of practical philosophy reached millions of readers.

Kathleen Norris.bio: Kathleen Norris is an American poet and essayist whose bestselling memoirs, including 'Dakota: A Spiritual Geography' (1993) and 'Amazing Grace: A Vocabulary of Faith' (1998), explore faith and life on the Great Plains.

Anne Bronte.bio: Anne Brontë, English novelist and poet, the youngest of the Brontë sisters. Writing as Acton Bell, she published Agnes Grey and The Tenant of Wildfell Hall, a landmark of early feminist fiction.

Arthur Rubinstein.bio: Polish-born American classical pianist, widely regarded as one of the greatest Chopin interpreters of the 20th century. His career spanned eight decades and he remained a beloved concert figure into his nineties.

Sogyal Rinpoche.bio: Sogyal Rinpoche was a Tibetan Buddhist teacher best known for The Tibetan Book of Living and Dying (1992), which introduced Tibetan teachings on death and dying to a wide Western audience. He founded the Rigpa international network of Buddhist centres.

Dennis Kimbro.bio: Dennis Kimbro is an American author and motivational speaker known for Think and Grow Rich: A Black Choice, written with Napoleon Hill, and What Makes the Great Great.

William Penn.role: English Quaker and founder of Pennsylvania
William Penn.bio: William Penn was an English Quaker, philosopher and entrepreneur who founded the Province of Pennsylvania as a refuge of religious tolerance. His writings, including No Cross, No Crown and Fruits of Solitude, reflect his pacifism and democratic principles.

Robert Lynd.bio: Robert Lynd was an Irish journalist and essayist who wrote for decades under the pen name 'Y.Y.' His gentle, humorous essays on everyday life were collected in books such as The Pleasures of Ignorance.

Robert Fulghum.bio: Robert Fulghum is an American author and Unitarian Universalist minister best known for All I Really Need to Know I Learned in Kindergarten (1986), a bestselling collection of reflective essays.

Tom Lehrer.bio: Tom Lehrer is an American singer-songwriter, satirist and mathematician famous for his humorous, sharply satirical songs of the 1950s and 1960s, including 'The Elements' and 'Poisoning Pigeons in the Park'. He also taught mathematics at Harvard and other universities.

Alfred Sheinwold.bio: American bridge expert whose syndicated newspaper column ran for decades. He wrote the classic 5 Weeks to Winning Bridge (1949) and co-created the Kaplan-Sheinwold bidding system.

Sri Chinmoy.bio: Sri Chinmoy was an Indian spiritual teacher who moved to New York in 1964 and taught meditation in the West. He wrote prolifically on spirituality and was also known as an artist, musician, poet and athlete who founded the Sri Chinmoy Marathon Team.

James Freeman Clarke.bio: James Freeman Clarke was an American Unitarian minister, theologian and author, and a figure in the transcendentalist circle. He founded the Church of the Disciples in Boston and promoted religious tolerance.

Anais Nin.bio: Anaïs Nin, French-born American diarist and novelist. She is celebrated for her multi-volume Diary, begun when she was eleven, and for works such as Delta of Venus.

Sydney Smith.bio: Sydney Smith was an English clergyman and writer celebrated as one of the great wits of his day. He co-founded the Edinburgh Review in 1802 and was famed for his humorous essays, letters and celebrated sermons.

Mary Kay Ash.bio: Mary Kay Ash founded Mary Kay Cosmetics (now Mary Kay Inc.) in 1963 with $5,000, building it into one of the world's largest direct sellers of skin care and cosmetics through a network of independent beauty consultants.

Lloyd Jones.bio: Lloyd Jones is a New Zealand novelist whose 'Mr Pip' (2006), set during the Bougainville civil war in Papua New Guinea, won the Commonwealth Writers' Prize and was shortlisted for the Booker Prize.

Ben Stein.bio: American writer, economist and actor, once a speechwriter for Presidents Nixon and Ford. He is famous as the droning teacher in Ferris Bueller's Day Off and as host of Win Ben Stein's Money.

Jacob Braude.bio: Jacob M. Braude was an American judge and humorist known for compiling popular collections of quotations, anecdotes and speaker's material, including Braude's Treasury of Wit and Humor.

Vince Lombardi.bio: Vince Lombardi was an American football coach who led the Green Bay Packers to five NFL championships in the 1960s, including victories in the first two Super Bowls. The Super Bowl trophy is named in his honour, and he remains a symbol of determination and leadership.

Oliver Wendell Holmes Sr..bio: Oliver Wendell Holmes Sr. was an American physician, poet and polymath, and one of the Fireside Poets. He coined the term 'anesthesia' and wrote the popular 'Breakfast-Table' series of essays and poems, including 'Old Ironsides'.

Robert Anthony.bio: Robert Anthony is an American self-help author and hypnotherapist known for books on confidence and positive thinking, including The Ultimate Secrets of Total Self-Confidence.

Washington Irving.bio: Washington Irving was an American short-story writer, essayist and historian best known for 'The Legend of Sleepy Hollow' and 'Rip Van Winkle'. He was among the first American writers to achieve international fame, and also wrote biographies and histories of Spain.

Jessamyn West.bio: Mary Jessamyn West was an American Quaker author known for The Friendly Persuasion (1945), stories of an Indiana Quaker family later adapted into the film Friendly Persuasion. She wrote novels, short stories and memoirs rooted in her Indiana and California upbringing.

Charlotte Perkins Gilman.bio: Charlotte Perkins Gilman was an American writer, lecturer and leading figure of the early feminist movement. She is best known for her semi-autobiographical short story "The Yellow Wallpaper" (1892) and the book Women and Economics (1898).

Margaret Runbeck.bio: Margaret Lee Runbeck was an American author known for her inspirational books and essays on hope, faith and resilience, and for her long association with the Salvation Army as a writer.

James Barrie.bio: Sir James Matthew Barrie was a Scottish novelist and playwright best remembered as the creator of Peter Pan, the boy who would not grow up. His play Peter Pan premiered in 1904 and became a timeless classic.

Everett Dirksen.bio: Everett Dirksen was an American politician who served as a US Senator from Illinois and Senate Minority Leader. Known for his mellifluous oratory, he played a key role in passing the Civil Rights Act of 1964.

Henry Miller.bio: Henry Miller was an American writer known for his autobiographical novels Tropic of Cancer and Tropic of Capricorn, which broke taboos of explicitness and were banned in the United States for decades.

Niels Bohr.bio: Niels Bohr was a Danish physicist who made foundational contributions to understanding atomic structure and quantum theory, for which he received the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1922. He founded the Institute of Theoretical Physics in Copenhagen.

Georg Lichtenberg.bio: Georg Christoph Lichtenberg was a German physicist, satirist and Anglophile who became the first German professor of experimental physics at Göttingen. He is best remembered for his posthumous aphorisms from his notebooks (the Sudelbücher), noted for their wit and sharp observation of human nature.

Charles Schwab.bio: Charles M. Schwab, American steel magnate. He rose to lead Carnegie Steel and then built Bethlehem Steel into one of the largest steel producers in the world.

Lou Holtz.bio: Lou Holtz is an American former football coach who led Notre Dame to a national championship in 1988 and finished his college coaching career with 249 wins. He later became a television analyst and motivational speaker.

Charles DeLint.bio: Charles de Lint, Dutch-born Canadian writer widely credited as a pioneer of urban fantasy. His Newford series, beginning with story collections such as Dreams Underfoot, blends myth and magic with contemporary city life.

Paavo Nurmi.bio: Paavo Nurmi was a Finnish middle- and long-distance runner known as the 'Flying Finn'. He won nine Olympic gold medals and set numerous world records in the 1920s.

Tryon Edwards.bio: Tryon Edwards was an American theologian and minister, a great-grandson of Jonathan Edwards. He is best remembered for compiling A Dictionary of Thoughts, a large collection of quotations and sentiments arranged by subject.

E. M. Forster.bio: Edward Morgan Forster was an English novelist known for A Room with a View, Howards End and A Passage to India, works examining class and connection in Edwardian society.

Lucille Ball.bio: Lucille Ball was an American actress and comedian whose sitcom 'I Love Lucy' (1951-57), co-starring her husband Desi Arnaz, became one of the most influential shows in television history. Through Desilu Productions she also became a pioneering television executive.

Elizabeth Arden.bio: Elizabeth Arden, born Florence Nightingale Graham in Canada, founded one of the world's leading cosmetics companies. She helped make makeup socially acceptable and built a global beauty empire.

Nikola Tesla.bio: Nikola Tesla was a Serbian-American inventor and electrical engineer known for his contributions to alternating current (AC) electricity supply systems. He held hundreds of patents and pioneered work on motors, radio and wireless energy.

Leo Aikman.bio: Leo Aikman was an American newspaper columnist and humorist, a longtime writer for The Atlanta Constitution, known for homespun observations on everyday life in the American South.

G. K. Chesterton.bio: Gilbert Keith Chesterton was an English writer, philosopher and critic whose work ranged from the Father Brown detective stories to theology and social commentary. His wit and paradox made him one of the most quoted writers of his era.

Denis Waitley.bio: Denis Waitley is an American motivational speaker and author of books on personal achievement, including The Psychology of Winning (1979).

Doug Larson.bio: Doug Larson was an American newspaper columnist and humorist whose syndicated column of witty one-liners appeared in papers across the United States.

Charles Lamb.bio: English essayist best known for the Essays of Elia, written under the pen name Elia. With his sister Mary he also wrote Tales from Shakespeare (1807), which introduced generations of children to the plays.

John Muir.bio: John Muir was a Scottish-American naturalist, author and early advocate for the preservation of wilderness in the United States. He co-founded the Sierra Club, and his writings helped inspire the creation of national parks including Yosemite.

William Ward.bio: William Ward, usually credited as William Arthur Ward, was an American writer of inspirational maxims and short poems, famous for lines about gratitude, attitude and possibility. His epigrams appeared in newspapers and magazines for decades and are widely quoted in motivational literature.

Michael Jordan.bio: Michael Jordan is an American former professional basketball player widely regarded as one of the greatest of all time. He led the Chicago Bulls to six NBA championships in the 1990s and won five MVP awards.

Ivy Baker Priest.bio: Ivy Baker Priest was an American public official who served as Treasurer of the United States under President Eisenhower, and later as treasurer of California. Her signature appeared on U.S. currency throughout the 1950s.

Ralph Blum.bio: Ralph H. Blum is an American writer best known for The Book of Runes (1982), which popularized the use of ancient Norse runes as a tool for guidance and self-reflection.

Walter Cronkite.bio: Walter Cronkite was an American broadcast journalist who anchored the CBS Evening News for nineteen years and was often called 'the most trusted man in America'. He reported on events from the Second World War to the Moon landing, signing off with 'And that's the way it is.'

Thomas Chalmers.bio: Thomas Chalmers, Scottish minister, theologian and social reformer. He led the evangelical party in the Disruption of 1843 and became the first Moderator of the Free Church of Scotland.

Joan Didion.bio: Joan Didion was an American writer and journalist famed for her cool, precise prose in essays like Slouching Towards Bethlehem and the memoir The Year of Magical Thinking, which won the National Book Award.

Mabel Newcomer.bio: Mabel Newcomer was an American economist and longtime professor at Vassar College, known for her studies of taxation and of women's higher education, including 'A Century of Higher Education for American Women' (1959).

Robert Graves.bio: Robert Graves was an English poet, novelist and classicist best known for the historical novel I, Claudius and his study of myth, The White Goddess. He also wrote the memoir Good-Bye to All That about his service in the First World War.

Francois de La Rochefoucauld.bio: François de La Rochefoucauld was a French author famed for his Maximes (1665), a collection of sharp, cynical reflections on human nature and self-interest.

Margaret Cousins.bio: Margaret Cousins was an Irish suffragist and theosophist who co-founded the Irish Women's Franchise League in 1908. She later settled in India, where she campaigned for women's education and voting rights and was imprisoned for her activism.

Catherine Pulsifer.bio: Canadian inspirational writer and the founder of Wow4U, a long-running website of motivational quotes, poems and short stories.

Margaret Mead.bio: Margaret Mead was an American cultural anthropologist whose fieldwork in Samoa and New Guinea, reported in 'Coming of Age in Samoa' (1928), made her one of the best-known social scientists of the twentieth century.

Remez Sasson.bio: Remez Sasson is an author and teacher of self-improvement and positive thinking who founded the website SuccessConsciousness. His books cover topics such as willpower, concentration and peace of mind.

Alan Watts.bio: British philosopher who popularised Eastern thought, including Zen Buddhism and Taoism, for Western audiences. His books include The Way of Zen (1957) and The Wisdom of Insecurity.

John Steinbeck.bio: John Steinbeck was an American novelist whose works, including 'The Grapes of Wrath' (1939), 'Of Mice and Men' (1937) and 'East of Eden' (1952), portray the lives of working people in California. He received the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1962.

Eknath Easwaran.bio: Eknath Easwaran was an Indian-born spiritual teacher and translator of the Bhagavad Gita, the Upanishads and the Dhammapada. He founded the Blue Mountain Center of Meditation in California.

Norman Schwarzkopf.bio: H. Norman Schwarzkopf was a United States Army general who commanded Coalition forces during the Gulf War of 1990-91, leading Operation Desert Storm against Iraq.

Julie Morgenstern.bio: Julie Morgenstern is an American organising and productivity consultant and the author of 'Organizing from the Inside Out' (1998) and 'Never Check E-Mail in the Morning' (2005). She founded the consulting firm Task Masters, later Julie Morgenstern Enterprises.

Harry Kemp.bio: Harry Kemp was an American poet, playwright and novelist known as the 'tramp poet' for his years of wandering. His memoir Tramping on Life (1922) chronicled his bohemian life on the road and at sea.

Henry Wadsworth Longfellow.bio: Henry Wadsworth Longfellow was an American poet and educator, among the most popular poets of his century. He wrote Paul Revere's Ride, The Song of Hiawatha and Evangeline, and produced the first American translation of Dante's Divine Comedy.

Daisaku Ikeda.bio: Daisaku Ikeda was a Japanese Buddhist philosopher, educator and peace activist who led the Soka Gakkai lay Buddhist movement and founded Soka University. He wrote extensively on Buddhism, dialogue and peace.

Rene Descartes.bio: Rene Descartes was a French philosopher and mathematician regarded as the father of modern Western philosophy. His statement 'I think, therefore I am' and his Discourse on Method laid groundwork for rationalism, and he also created analytic geometry.

Amelia Earhart.bio: American aviation pioneer and the first woman to fly solo nonstop across the Atlantic Ocean, in 1932. She disappeared over the Pacific in 1937 while attempting to circumnavigate the globe.

Jimmy Dean.bio: Jimmy Dean was an American country music singer and television host who founded the Jimmy Dean sausage company. His 1961 hit 'Big Bad John' topped the charts and won a Grammy Award.

George Allen.bio: George Herbert Allen was an American football coach best known for leading the Los Angeles Rams and the Washington Redskins. Famous for the motto 'The future is now,' he was inducted into the Pro Football Hall of Fame in 2002.

Joseph Roux.bio: Joseph Roux was a French parish priest, philologist and writer in the Corrèze region, remembered for his aphorisms and reflections on rural life, faith and human nature.

Bernice Reagon.bio: Bernice Johnson Reagon, American singer, composer and historian. A Freedom Singer in the civil rights movement, she founded the a cappella ensemble Sweet Honey in the Rock in 1973.

Henri Bergson.bio: Henri Bergson was a French philosopher influential for his ideas on time, memory and creative evolution. He received the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1927.

David Brinkley.bio: David Brinkley was an American television journalist who co-anchored NBC's Huntley-Brinkley Report and later hosted ABC's This Week. His dry delivery made him one of the most recognisable figures in broadcast news.

Pierre Auguste Renoir.bio: Pierre-Auguste Renoir was a French artist and a leading painter of the Impressionist movement. Known for vibrant scenes of Parisian life such as Dance at Le Moulin de la Galette, he later turned to portraiture and the female nude.

Bob Newhart.bio: American stand-up comedian and actor whose deadpan delivery made The Button-Down Mind (1960) a chart-topping comedy album. He starred in The Bob Newhart Show and Newhart, and appeared in films such as Elf.

Rita Mae Brown.bio: Rita Mae Brown is an American feminist writer best known for the groundbreaking novel Rubyfruit Jungle (1973) and the Mrs. Murphy mystery series, co-credited to her cat.

Lululemon.bio: Lululemon Athletica is a Canadian athletic apparel company founded in Vancouver in 1998, best known for yoga clothing and for the motivational manifesto printed on its products and shopping bags.

Kin Hubbard.bio: Frank McKinney Hubbard, known as 'Kin' Hubbard, was an American cartoonist and humorist who created the comic strip 'Abe Martin of Brown County'. His folksy aphorisms about politics and everyday life were syndicated in newspapers across the United States.

Mary Morrissey.bio: Mary Manin Morrissey is an American author, minister and transformational speaker, and founder of the Life Mastery Institute. Her books include 'Building Your Field of Dreams' (1996) and 'No Less Than Greatness' (2001).

Peter Elbow.bio: Peter Elbow is an American scholar of rhetoric and writing known for Writing Without Teachers (1973), which popularized freewriting as a way to generate and develop ideas.

Rudolf Arnheim.bio: Rudolf Arnheim was a German-American art theorist and psychologist of perception. His book Art and Visual Perception (1954) applied Gestalt psychology to the visual arts and influenced generations of artists and designers.

William Ellery Channing.bio: William Ellery Channing, American clergyman and the leading voice of Unitarian Christianity in the early 19th century. His sermons and essays championed self-culture, abolition and social reform.

Cervantes.bio: Miguel de Cervantes Saavedra, Spanish writer and author of Don Quixote (1605, 1615), often called the first modern novel and one of the greatest works of world literature.

Tehyi Hsieh.bio: Tehyi Hsieh was a Chinese philosopher and writer whose brief aphorisms on the mind, thought and character are widely quoted.

Japanese proverb.bio: A traditional Japanese proverb, reflecting centuries of folk wisdom.

Charles Swindoll.bio: Charles R. 'Chuck' Swindoll, American evangelical pastor and author. He founded the radio programme Insight for Living and served as president of Dallas Theological Seminary.

Cynthia Ozick.bio: Cynthia Ozick is an American novelist, short-story writer and essayist known for works such as The Shawl and her essays on literature and Jewish life.

Lena Horne.bio: Lena Horne was an American singer, actress and civil rights activist whose career spanned more than seven decades, from the Cotton Club and Hollywood musicals to a Tony Award-winning one-woman Broadway show in 1981.

Tom Peters.bio: Tom Peters is an American writer on business management best known as co-author of In Search of Excellence (1982), one of the best-selling management books ever published. He has written and lectured extensively on corporate excellence and innovation.

Shakti Gawain.bio: Shakti Gawain was an American author and a pioneer of the New Age and personal development movements. Her 1978 book Creative Visualization popularized the use of mental imagery and affirmations.

Paul Cezanne.bio: Paul Cezanne was a French Post-Impressionist painter whose work laid the foundations for modern art. His explorations of geometric form in landscapes, portraits and still lifes profoundly influenced Picasso and Matisse.

Frank Tyger.bio: Frank Tyger was an American editorial cartoonist for The Times of Trenton, New Jersey, whose cartoons and aphorisms were widely reprinted.

Dorothy Thompson.bio: Dorothy Thompson was an American journalist and radio broadcaster, one of the most influential women in American journalism in the 1930s. She was expelled from Nazi Germany in 1934 for her reporting on Hitler.

T. S. Eliot.bio: Thomas Stearns Eliot, known as T. S. Eliot, was an American-born British poet and critic, author of The Love Song of J. Alfred Prufrock, The Waste Land and Four Quartets. He received the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1948 and is regarded as a central figure of modernist poetry.

John Dewey.bio: John Dewey was an American philosopher, psychologist and educational reformer, a central figure in pragmatism. His ideas on learning by doing profoundly shaped progressive education.

George Orwell.bio: George Orwell (born Eric Arthur Blair) was an English novelist, essayist and critic. His dystopian novel Nineteen Eighty-Four and the allegory Animal Farm made terms like 'Big Brother' and 'thoughtcrime' part of the language.

John Petit-Senn.bio: Jean-Antoine Petit-Senn was a Swiss poet and writer from Geneva, best remembered for his collections of maxims and reflections, 'Bluettes et boutades' (1846).

Mary Wollstonecraft.bio: Mary Wollstonecraft was an English writer and advocate of women's rights, best known for A Vindication of the Rights of Woman (1792). She argued that women are not naturally inferior to men but appear so because of a lack of education. She was the mother of Frankenstein author Mary Shelley.

Sheldon Kopp.bio: Sheldon B. Kopp was an American psychotherapist and author known for If You Meet the Buddha on the Road, Kill Him! (1972), a candid book about psychotherapy and self-discovery.

Satchel Paige.bio: Leroy 'Satchel' Paige was an American baseball pitcher who starred for decades in the Negro leagues before joining Major League Baseball at about age 42. He is regarded as one of the greatest pitchers in the game's history.

Billy Wilder.bio: Austrian-born American filmmaker, one of Hollywood's most versatile directors. His classics include Double Indemnity, Sunset Boulevard, Some Like It Hot and The Apartment, which won the Academy Award for Best Picture.

Niccolo Machiavelli.bio: Niccolo Machiavelli was an Italian diplomat and political philosopher of the Renaissance. His treatise The Prince, published after his death, examined the acquisition and maintenance of political power and made his name a byword for political realism.

Henry Ward Beecher.bio: Henry Ward Beecher was an American Congregationalist clergyman, social reformer and speaker, famous as the minister of Plymouth Church in Brooklyn. He was a leading abolitionist and one of the most influential religious voices of 19th-century America.

James Faust.bio: James E. Faust was an American religious leader who served as Second Counselor in the First Presidency of The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints from 1995 until his death. He was earlier a Utah legislator and president of the Utah State Bar.

Hasidic saying.bio: A traditional saying from Hasidic Judaism, the mystical movement founded in 18th-century Eastern Europe.

Joseph Campbell.bio: Joseph Campbell was an American mythologist and professor whose 'The Hero with a Thousand Faces' (1949) described the hero's journey pattern found in myths worldwide. His televised conversations with Bill Moyers, 'The Power of Myth' (1988), brought his ideas to a wide audience.

Dhammapada.bio: The Dhammapada is a collection of sayings of the Buddha in verse, one of the best-known texts of the Pali Canon of Theravada Buddhism.

Fannie Hamer.bio: Fannie Lou Hamer was an American civil rights activist who co-founded the Mississippi Freedom Democratic Party and challenged the state's all-white delegation at the 1964 Democratic National Convention. Her testimony about being beaten for registering to vote drew national attention.

Babatunde Olatunji.bio: Nigerian master drummer whose album Drums of Passion (1959) introduced African drumming to American audiences. He founded a centre for African culture in Harlem and taught drumming for decades.

Tony Blair.bio: Tony Blair is a British politician who served as Prime Minister of the United Kingdom from 1997 to 2007, leading the Labour Party to three consecutive general election victories. After leaving office he founded the Tony Blair Institute for Global Change.

Ray Bradbury.bio: Ray Bradbury was an American author and screenwriter known for the dystopian novel Fahrenheit 451 and The Martian Chronicles. His work blended science fiction, fantasy and horror with a distinctive lyrical style.

Herbert Swope.bio: Herbert Bayard Swope was an American journalist and editor, executive editor of the New York World, whose reporters won some of the first Pulitzer Prizes. He is credited with coining the term 'Cold War.'

Orison Marden.bio: Orison Swett Marden was an American inspirational author and founder of Success magazine in 1897. His books, such as Pushing to the Front, were early classics of the self-help genre.

Sam Levenson.bio: Sam Levenson was an American humorist, teacher and television personality known for gentle, family-centered humour. His poem 'Time Tested Beauty Tips', written for his granddaughter, became widely beloved.

Doris Mortman.bio: Doris Mortman is an American novelist known for romantic suspense novels including First Born and The Wild Rose.

Mortimer Adler.bio: Mortimer J. Adler was an American philosopher and educator who championed the Great Books of the Western World program. He chaired the board of editors of Encyclopaedia Britannica and founded the Paideia Proposal for school reform.

Tenzin Gyatso.bio: Tenzin Gyatso is the 14th Dalai Lama, the spiritual leader of Tibetan Buddhism, recognised as the reincarnation of his predecessor at the age of two. He has lived in exile in India since 1959 and received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1989 for his nonviolent advocacy for Tibet.

William Channing.bio: William Ellery Channing was an American Unitarian preacher and theologian, the leading voice of Unitarian Christianity in the early nineteenth century. His sermons and essays championed liberal religion, abolition and social reform.

Alphonse Karr.bio: Jean-Baptiste Alphonse Karr, French critic, journalist and novelist. He coined the famous epigram that the more things change, the more they stay the same.

W. H. Auden.bio: W. H. Auden was an English-American poet regarded as one of the greatest writers of the twentieth century, author of poems such as 'Funeral Blues' and 'Musée des Beaux Arts'. His work ranges across politics, love, religion and psychology in a dazzling variety of forms.

Margaret Laurence.bio: Margaret Laurence was one of Canada's most celebrated novelists, author of the Manawaka cycle of books set in a fictional prairie town, including 'The Stone Angel' (1964) and 'The Diviners' (1974).

Vincent Lombardi.bio: Vincent Thomas Lombardi was an American football coach who led the Green Bay Packers to five NFL championships in the 1960s, including the first two Super Bowls. The Super Bowl trophy bears his name, and his sayings on winning and effort are quoted far beyond sport.

Elisabeth Kubler-Ross.bio: Elisabeth Kübler-Ross was a Swiss-American psychiatrist whose book On Death and Dying (1969) introduced the five stages of grief. Her work transformed the care of terminally ill patients.

Anne Lindbergh.bio: Anne Morrow Lindbergh, American aviator and author who flew survey routes with her husband Charles Lindbergh. Her reflective bestseller Gift from the Sea (1955) remains widely loved.

Dale Carnegie.bio: Dale Carnegie was an American writer and lecturer on self-improvement and public speaking. His book How to Win Friends and Influence People (1936) became one of the best-selling books of all time.

Nathaniel Hawthorne.bio: Nathaniel Hawthorne was an American novelist and short story writer known for The Scarlet Letter and The House of the Seven Gables. His works explore sin, guilt and the moral history of Puritan New England.

Caroline Myss.bio: American author and speaker on spirituality and energy medicine. Her bestsellers include Anatomy of the Spirit (1996) and Sacred Contracts.

William James.bio: William James was an American philosopher and psychologist, regarded as a founder of modern psychology and a leading thinker of pragmatism. His works include The Principles of Psychology (1890), The Varieties of Religious Experience and Pragmatism.

Uta Hagen.bio: Uta Hagen was a German-American actress and influential acting teacher, author of the classic manuals Respect for Acting and A Challenge for the Actor. She originated the role of Martha in Edward Albee's Who's Afraid of Virginia Woolf? and co-founded the HB Studio in New York.

Viktor Frankl.bio: Viktor Frankl was an Austrian psychiatrist and Holocaust survivor who founded logotherapy, a form of psychotherapy centred on the search for meaning. His book Man's Search for Meaning (1946), drawn from his experiences in Nazi concentration camps, has sold millions of copies worldwide.

Edward de Bono.bio: Edward de Bono was a Maltese physician and author who coined the term "lateral thinking" and created the Six Thinking Hats method for structured problem-solving.

Amy Tan.bio: American novelist best known for The Joy Luck Club (1989), which portrays the lives of Chinese-American mothers and daughters. Her other novels include The Kitchen God's Wife and The Bonesetter's Daughter.

Stephen Covey.bio: Stephen R. Covey was an American educator and businessman best known for The 7 Habits of Highly Effective People (1989), one of the best-selling self-help books of all time. He co-founded the FranklinCovey consulting company and taught organisational leadership.

Paul Graham.bio: Paul Graham is an English-born American computer scientist, essayist and venture capitalist. He co-founded the startup accelerator Y Combinator and is known for essays on programming, startups and language design, as well as the book Hackers and Painters.

Chuck Norris.bio: Chuck Norris is an American martial artist and actor who rose to fame in action films and the television series Walker, Texas Ranger. He won multiple karate championships before turning to acting.

Amy Bloom.bio: American writer and psychotherapist. She is known for the story collection Come to Me and novels such as Away (2007) and White Houses (2018).

Keshavan Nair.bio: Keshavan Nair is an Indian-born author and consultant whose book 'A Higher Standard of Leadership: Lessons from the Life of Gandhi' (1994) applies Gandhi's principles to modern organisations and leadership.

Ingrid Bergman.bio: Ingrid Bergman was a Swedish actress who starred in Casablanca, Gaslight and Notorious, winning three Academy Awards. She is regarded as one of the greatest screen actresses of all time.

Thornton Wilder.bio: Thornton Wilder was an American playwright and novelist who won three Pulitzer Prizes, for the novel The Bridge of San Luis Rey and the plays Our Town and The Skin of Our Teeth. Our Town remains one of the most performed American plays.

James Oppenheim.bio: James Oppenheim was an American poet, novelist and editor, founder of the literary magazine The Seven Arts. His poem 'Bread and Roses' (1911) became a rallying cry of the labour movement.

Martha Washington.role: First First Lady of the United States
Martha Washington.bio: Martha Washington was the wife of George Washington and the first First Lady of the United States (1789-1797). She managed the Mount Vernon estate and, during the Revolutionary War, spent winters with the Continental Army supporting the troops.

Margaret Wander Bonanno.bio: Margaret Wander Bonanno was an American science fiction author best known for her Star Trek novels, including 'Dwellers in the Crucible' (1985) and 'Strangers from the Sky' (1987).

Joe Paterno.bio: Joe Paterno was the head football coach of the Penn State Nittany Lions for 46 seasons, becoming the winningest coach in major college football history. His career ended in 2011 amid the Sandusky scandal.

Demosthenes.bio: Demosthenes was an Athenian statesman and the greatest orator of ancient Greece. His speeches urged Athens to resist the rising power of Philip II of Macedon.

Gail Sheehy.bio: Gail Sheehy was an American author and journalist best known for Passages (1976), a bestselling study of adult life stages. She profiled major political figures for magazines including Vanity Fair.

Mohandas Gandhi.bio: Mohandas Karamchand Gandhi, known as Mahatma Gandhi, led India's movement for independence from British rule through nonviolent civil disobedience. His philosophy of satyagraha inspired civil rights movements around the world. He was assassinated in 1948.

John Locke.bio: John Locke was an English philosopher and physician whose ideas on empiricism, natural rights and government by consent shaped the Enlightenment and modern liberal thought. His major works include 'An Essay Concerning Human Understanding' (1689) and 'Two Treatises of Government' (1689).

Soren Kierkegaard.bio: Søren Kierkegaard was a Danish philosopher, theologian and poet widely regarded as the first existentialist thinker. His works, including Fear and Trembling and Either/Or, explored faith, anxiety, despair and the individual's subjective relationship to truth.

David Eddings.bio: David Eddings was an American author of epic fantasy, best known for The Belgariad and The Malloreon series, written with his wife Leigh Eddings.

David McCullough.bio: David McCullough was an American historian and two-time Pulitzer Prize winner, for Truman (1992) and John Adams (2001). He was also known as the narrator of documentary films including Ken Burns's The Civil War.

William Blake.bio: William Blake was an English poet, painter and printmaker whose illuminated books, including Songs of Innocence and of Experience and The Marriage of Heaven and Hell, were largely unrecognised in his lifetime. He is now considered a seminal figure of Romantic poetry and visual art.

Euripides.bio: Euripides was an Athenian tragedian, one of the three great playwrights of classical Greek theatre alongside Aeschylus and Sophocles. His plays, including Medea and The Bacchae, explored psychology and questioned traditional myths.

William Sloane Coffin.bio: William Sloane Coffin Jr. was an American Christian clergyman and peace activist who served as chaplain of Yale University and senior minister of Riverside Church in New York. A former CIA officer, he became a leading voice of the civil rights and anti-war movements.

Andy Rooney.bio: American radio and television writer best known for A Few Minutes with Andy Rooney, his closing segment on CBS's 60 Minutes from 1978 to 2011. His humorous essays on everyday life made him a household voice.

Paul Tillich.bio: Paul Tillich was a German-American theologian and philosopher whose works, including The Courage to Be and his three-volume Systematic Theology, described faith as 'ultimate concern'.

William Burroughs.bio: William S. Burroughs was an American writer and a leading figure of the Beat Generation, best known for the novel Naked Lunch (1959). His experimental cut-up technique and themes of addiction and control systems influenced generations of writers and artists.

Anne Lamott.bio: American novelist and nonfiction writer known for her candid, humorous work on faith and writing. Her books include the writing classic Bird by Bird (1994) and the spiritual memoir Traveling Mercies.

Robert Kennedy.bio: Robert F. Kennedy was an American politician who served as U.S. Attorney General and then as a U.S. Senator from New York. He was assassinated in 1968 while campaigning for the Democratic presidential nomination.

Richard Whately.bio: Richard Whately was an English academic and cleric who became Archbishop of Dublin. He revived the study of logic in works such as Elements of Logic and wrote widely on economics and rhetoric.

Marsha Petrie Sue.bio: Marsha Petrie Sue is an American author and professional speaker on communication and workplace behaviour, best known for 'Toxic People: Decontaminate Difficult People at Work Without Using Weapons or Duct Tape'.

Alexander Pope.bio: English poet and master of the heroic couplet. His works include An Essay on Criticism, The Rape of the Lock and An Essay on Man, along with celebrated translations of Homer.

Abraham Maslow.bio: American psychologist who founded humanistic psychology. He is best known for his hierarchy of needs, set out in Motivation and Personality (1954), and for popularising the concept of self-actualisation.

Zig Ziglar.bio: Zig Ziglar was an American author and motivational speaker who became one of the most influential sales and personal-development trainers of the twentieth century. His book See You at the Top and his famous line 'Your attitude, not your aptitude, will determine your altitude' reached millions.

Frances de Sales.bio: Francis de Sales was a French Catholic bishop of Geneva and a Doctor of the Church, canonised as a saint. His Introduction to the Devout Life (1609) became a classic of Christian spirituality.

George Matthew Adams.bio: George Matthew Adams was an American newspaper columnist and founder of a newspaper syndication service. His daily column of short inspirational essays was carried by dozens of newspapers.

Robert M. Pirsig.bio: Robert M. Pirsig was an American writer and philosopher best known for Zen and the Art of Motorcycle Maintenance (1974), a philosophical novel exploring the concept of Quality that became a countercultural classic.

Albert Gray.bio: American insurance executive with the Prudential Insurance Company of America. He is remembered for his 1940 address The Common Denominator of Success, a classic of sales and success literature.

Grandma Moses.bio: Anna Mary Robertson Moses, known as Grandma Moses, was an American folk artist who began painting in earnest at the age of 78. Her scenes of rural American life became beloved worldwide, and she painted more than 1,500 canvases.

Swedish proverb.bio: A traditional Swedish saying, passed down through generations as part of Sweden's folk wisdom.

Felix Adler.bio: Felix Adler was a German-American educator and philosopher who founded the Ethical Culture movement in 1876, emphasising ethics and social reform outside organised religion. He became the first professor of political and social ethics at Columbia University.

Joseph Joubert.bio: Joseph Joubert was a French moralist and essayist whose notebooks of reflections on literature, philosophy and life were published posthumously as 'Pensées' (1842).

Ella Fitzgerald.bio: Ella Fitzgerald was an American jazz singer known as the "First Lady of Song", celebrated for her pure tone, scat singing and interpretations of the Great American Songbook. She won 13 Grammy Awards.

Ralph Marston.bio: Ralph Marston is an American motivational writer best known as the publisher of The Daily Motivator, a long-running source of short positive-thinking messages.

Lewis Cass.bio: Lewis Cass was an American military officer and politician who served as governor of Michigan Territory, U.S. senator, secretary of war under Andrew Jackson and secretary of state under James Buchanan. He was the Democratic nominee for president in 1848.

Danilo Dolci.bio: Danilo Dolci was an Italian social activist, sociologist and poet who worked with the poor of Sicily using nonviolent methods. Sometimes called the "Gandhi of Sicily", he was nominated for the Nobel Peace Prize.

Franz Liszt.bio: Franz Liszt was a Hungarian composer, pianist and conductor, one of the most celebrated virtuosos of the nineteenth century. He invented the symphonic poem and transformed piano technique.

Corita Kent.bio: Corita Kent, born Frances Elizabeth Kent, was an American artist and educator who entered the Sisters of the Immaculate Heart of Mary. Her colourful silk-screen prints combined pop art with messages of love and social justice.

Alice Walker.bio: American writer whose novel The Color Purple (1982) won the Pulitzer Prize for Fiction and the National Book Award. She coined the term womanist and helped revive interest in Zora Neale Hurston.

Charles Chesnutt.bio: Charles W. Chesnutt, African American author and essayist. His story collection The Conjure Woman (1899) and novel The Marrow of Tradition (1901) confronted race and identity in the post-slavery South.

Elizabeth Kenny.bio: Sister Elizabeth Kenny was an Australian nurse who developed a controversial method of treating polio through physical therapy rather than immobilisation. Her clinics in Australia and the United States helped change polio care.

Edward Young.bio: Edward Young was an English poet best known for Night Thoughts (1742–1745), a long poem on death and immortality that was hugely popular across Europe.

Joyce Brothers.bio: Dr Joyce Brothers was an American psychologist who became a pioneering television and radio advice personality after winning the quiz show 'The $64,000 Question' in 1955. She wrote a widely syndicated newspaper column and several bestselling books on relationships and behaviour.

Gordon Hinckley.bio: Gordon B. Hinckley served as the 15th president of The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints from 1995 until his death. He oversaw extensive temple building and the church's global growth, and received the Presidential Medal of Freedom in 2004.

Edmond Rostand.bio: Edmond Rostand was a French playwright best known for Cyrano de Bergerac (1897), one of the most famous plays in French theatre.

Samuel Taylor Coleridge.bio: Samuel Taylor Coleridge was an English poet and critic, a founder of the Romantic movement alongside William Wordsworth. His poems include 'The Rime of the Ancient Mariner' and 'Kubla Khan', and his Biographia Literaria is a landmark of literary criticism.

Simone Weil.bio: Simone Weil was a French philosopher, mystic and political activist. Her posthumously published works, including Gravity and Grace and The Need for Roots, combine rigorous thought with deep spiritual and social concern.

Jean Lacordaire.bio: Jean-Baptiste Henri Lacordaire was a French Dominican friar and celebrated preacher who revived the Dominican Order in France after the Revolution. His conferences at Notre-Dame drew huge audiences.

Moliere.bio: Moliere, the stage name of Jean-Baptiste Poquelin, was a French playwright and actor regarded as one of the greatest writers of comedy in Western literature. His plays include Tartuffe, The Misanthrope and The School for Wives.

Woody Guthrie.bio: Woody Guthrie was an American folk singer-songwriter whose songs about the Dust Bowl, migration and social justice, including 'This Land Is Your Land', shaped American folk music. He wrote hundreds of songs and influenced generations of musicians, including Bob Dylan.

Forrest Church.bio: Forrest Church was an American Unitarian Universalist minister and theologian who led the Unitarian Church of All Souls in New York City. He wrote widely on liberal religion, American history and facing mortality.
