Coco Chanel.bio: Coco Chanel was a French fashion designer and founder of the Chanel brand. She transformed women's fashion with designs such as the little black dress and launched the perfume Chanel No. 5.

Ambrose Bierce.bio: American short-story writer, satirist and Civil War veteran, author of An Occurrence at Owl Creek Bridge and The Devil's Dictionary (1906). He disappeared in Mexico in 1914 while observing the revolution.

Etty Hillesum.bio: Etty Hillesum was a Dutch Jewish diarist and letter-writer whose writings from Amsterdam and the Westerbork transit camp became a moving record of spiritual life under Nazi occupation. She was murdered at Auschwitz in 1943.

Jamie Paolinetti.bio: Jamie Paolinetti is an American former professional road racing cyclist who competed through the 1990s. He later became a filmmaker, directing documentaries about professional cycling.

Joe Namath.bio: Joe Namath, nicknamed 'Broadway Joe,' was an American football quarterback who led the New York Jets to victory in Super Bowl III after famously guaranteeing the win. He was inducted into the Pro Football Hall of Fame in 1985.

Pierre Abelard.bio: Pierre Abelard was a French scholastic philosopher and theologian famous for his method of questioning in Sic et Non and for his ill-fated love affair with Heloise, recorded in their letters.

Dr. David M. Burns.bio: David D. Burns is an American psychiatrist and author of Feeling Good: The New Mood Therapy, a popular book on cognitive behavioural techniques for treating depression.

Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart.bio: Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart was an Austrian composer of the Classical era, a child prodigy who composed more than six hundred works before his death at thirty-five. His operas, symphonies and concertos, including Don Giovanni and The Marriage of Figaro, are cornerstones of Western music.

Saul Alinsky.bio: Saul Alinsky was an American community organizer regarded as the founder of modern community organizing. His book Rules for Radicals (1971) remains an influential manual for activists and organizers.

Charles A. Lindbergh.bio: American aviator who made the first solo nonstop transatlantic flight, from New York to Paris, in the Spirit of St. Louis in 1927. The feat made him one of the most famous people in the world.

Robert Brault.bio: Robert Brault is an American freelance writer and aphorist known for short, widely quoted observations on everyday life, many of which first appeared in his newspaper writing.

John Lubbock.bio: John Lubbock, 1st Baron Avebury, was an English banker, politician, naturalist and author who as an MP introduced the Bank Holidays Act 1871. He wrote popular works on science and the conduct of life, including 'The Pleasures of Life' (1887).

Alfred Adler.bio: Austrian physician and psychotherapist who founded the school of individual psychology. He introduced influential concepts including the inferiority complex and the importance of birth order.

Robert Schuller.bio: Robert H. Schuller was an American Christian televangelist and pastor who founded the Crystal Cathedral in California and hosted the Hour of Power broadcast. He preached a message of 'possibility thinking'.

Stephen Kaggwa.bio: Stephen Kaggwa is a Ugandan motivational speaker widely quoted for the line 'Try and fail, but don't fail to try.'

Percy Shelley.bio: Percy Bysshe Shelley was an English Romantic poet known for lyrics such as 'Ozymandias', 'Ode to the West Wind' and Adonais. He was married to Mary Shelley, author of Frankenstein.

Korean proverb.bio: A traditional Korean proverb - a folk saying handed down through generations in Korea.

Bertrand Russell.bio: British philosopher, logician and social critic, co-author of Principia Mathematica. He won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1950 and wrote the popular History of Western Philosophy.

Douglas Adams.bio: Douglas Adams was an English author best known for The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy, which began as a BBC radio comedy and became a series of bestselling books. He also wrote the Dirk Gently detective novels.

Muriel Rukeyser.bio: Muriel Rukeyser was an American poet and political activist known for poetry that combined social protest with lyric intensity, including The Book of the Dead about the Hawk's Nest Tunnel disaster.

Will Durant.bio: Will Durant was an American historian and philosopher best known for The Story of Civilization, the eleven-volume history he wrote with his wife Ariel Durant. Their work won the Pulitzer Prize for General Nonfiction in 1968.

John Barrymore.bio: John Barrymore was an American actor of stage and screen, acclaimed for his Shakespearean roles, including Hamlet, and films such as Dr. Jekyll and Mr. Hyde and Grand Hotel. He was a member of the famous Barrymore theatrical family.

Winifred Holtby.bio: Winifred Holtby was an English novelist and journalist best known for South Riding, her posthumously published novel of local government in Yorkshire, which won the James Tait Black Memorial Prize. A feminist and social reformer, she was a close friend of Vera Brittain.

Richard Garriott.bio: Richard Garriott is a British-American video game developer best known for creating the Ultima series of role-playing games as 'Lord British'. In 2008 he flew to the International Space Station as a private space tourist.

Harriet Lerner.bio: Harriet Lerner is an American psychologist and psychotherapist known for her work on women's psychology and relationships. Her best-known book, The Dance of Anger (1985), has sold millions of copies.

Maori proverb.bio: A traditional proverb of the Maori, the Indigenous people of New Zealand (Aotearoa), handed down through generations.

Jack Buck.bio: Jack Buck was an American sportscaster, the beloved voice of the St. Louis Cardinals for nearly five decades. He was inducted into the broadcasters' wing of the Baseball Hall of Fame in 1987.

Whoopi Goldberg.bio: Whoopi Goldberg is an American comedian, actress and television host, one of the few entertainers to win an Emmy, Grammy, Oscar and Tony Award. She starred in The Color Purple and Ghost, and has co-hosted the talk show The View since 2007.

Henry Reed.bio: Henry Reed was a British poet and radio dramatist best known for the war poem 'Naming of Parts' (1942). He also wrote popular radio plays featuring the comic character Hilda Tablet.

Pat Riley.bio: Pat Riley is an American professional basketball executive and former coach who led the Los Angeles Lakers to four NBA championships in the 1980s and later won another title coaching the Miami Heat.

Galileo Galilei.bio: Galileo Galilei was an Italian astronomer and physicist whose telescopic observations supported the heliocentric model of the solar system. His defence of Copernican astronomy brought him into conflict with the Catholic Church.

Margaret Wheatley.bio: Margaret J. Wheatley is an American writer and consultant on organisational behaviour whose 'Leadership and the New Science' (1992) applies ideas from chaos theory and biology to leadership. She is a co-founder of the Berkana Institute.

George Eliot.bio: George Eliot was the pen name of Mary Ann Evans, one of the leading English novelists of the Victorian era. Her works, including Middlemarch, Adam Bede and The Mill on the Floss, are celebrated for their realism and psychological depth.

Sarah Breathnach.bio: Sarah Ban Breathnach is an American author best known for Simple Abundance (1995), a bestselling daybook on gratitude and living authentically that was popularized through Oprah Winfrey's show.

Lisa Alther.bio: Lisa Alther is an American novelist best known for 'Kinflicks' (1976), a comic coming-of-age bestseller, and later novels including 'Other Women' (1984), as well as the nonfiction history 'Blood Feud' (2012).

Walter Benjamin.bio: Walter Benjamin was a German philosopher and cultural critic associated with the Frankfurt School. His essay 'The Work of Art in the Age of Mechanical Reproduction' remains a landmark of media theory; he died in 1940 while fleeing the Nazis.

Lama Yeshe.bio: Lama Thubten Yeshe was a Tibetan Buddhist lama who, with Lama Zopa Rinpoche, co-founded Kopan Monastery in Nepal and the Foundation for the Preservation of the Mahayana Tradition (FPMT). He was among the first Tibetan teachers to bring Buddhism to Western students.

Cardinal Retz.bio: Jean-François Paul de Gondi, Cardinal de Retz, French churchman and political intriguer during the Fronde uprising. His Memoirs are a celebrated classic of French literature, famed for their portraits and maxims.

E. E. Cummings.bio: Edward Estlin Cummings, known as e. e. cummings, was an American poet noted for his experimental syntax, punctuation and typography. He wrote nearly 3,000 poems as well as plays and essays.

Vaclav Havel.bio: Václav Havel was a Czech playwright, essayist and dissident who became the last President of Czechoslovakia and the first President of the Czech Republic after the Velvet Revolution. His plays and essays, including The Power of the Powerless, made him a symbol of resistance to communism.

Victoria Holt.bio: Victoria Holt was the best-known pen name of Eleanor Hibbert, a prolific British author of romantic suspense novels such as Mistress of Mellyn. Under her various pen names, including Jean Plaidy and Philippa Carr, she sold over a hundred million books.

Chuang Tzu.bio: Chuang Tzu (Zhuangzi) was an influential Chinese philosopher of the Warring States period and, with Laozi, a founder of Taoism. The book bearing his name is one of the foundational texts of Taoist thought.

Billie Armstrong.bio: Best known as Billie Joe Armstrong, the American singer, songwriter and guitarist who fronts the rock band Green Day. Albums such as Dookie and American Idiot made the band one of the defining acts of punk rock.

Alfred Korzybski.bio: Polish-American scholar who founded general semantics, presented in Science and Sanity (1933). He is famous for the maxim that the map is not the territory.

Alfred North Whitehead.bio: Alfred North Whitehead, English mathematician and philosopher. He co-authored Principia Mathematica with Bertrand Russell and later developed process philosophy in Process and Reality (1929).

Isocrates.bio: Isocrates was an ancient Greek rhetorician and educator in Athens, one of the ten Attic orators. His school of rhetoric influenced Western prose style and education for centuries.

Robert Orben.bio: Robert Orben was an American magician and comedy writer known for his joke books for speakers. He wrote material for comedian Red Skelton and served as a speechwriter for President Gerald Ford.

Hermann Hesse.bio: Hermann Hesse was a German-Swiss novelist and poet whose works explore self-discovery and spirituality, including Siddhartha, Steppenwolf and The Glass Bead Game. He received the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1946.

David Bader.bio: David M. Bader is an American writer known for humorous books such as Haikus for Jews (1999) and Zen Judaism.

David Rockefeller.bio: David Rockefeller was an American banker and philanthropist who led Chase Manhattan Bank. The youngest grandson of oil magnate John D. Rockefeller, he became a prominent figure in international finance and philanthropy.

Cavour.bio: Camillo Benso, Count of Cavour, Italian statesman who engineered the unification of Italy through diplomacy and statecraft. He became the first Prime Minister of the united Kingdom of Italy in 1861, shortly before his death.

Moncure Conway.bio: Moncure Daniel Conway was an American abolitionist, Unitarian clergyman and writer. He freed his family's slaves after inheriting them and became a prominent voice against slavery and for free thought.

Walt Disney.bio: Walt Disney was an American animator, film producer and entrepreneur who co-founded the Disney studio and created Mickey Mouse. He won a record 22 Academy Awards, built Disneyland in California, and transformed animation and family entertainment worldwide.

Norman Peale.bio: Norman Vincent Peale was an American minister and author best known for The Power of Positive Thinking (1952), a bestseller that promoted optimism and faith as keys to success and happiness.

Alexander the Great.bio: King of Macedon who, by the age of thirty, had conquered an empire stretching from Greece to Egypt and northwestern India. He founded more than twenty cities named Alexandria, the most famous in Egypt.

Theodore Rubin.bio: Theodore Isaac Rubin was an American psychiatrist and author of more than thirty books, including Compassion and Self-Hate (1975). His fiction and popular psychology writing explored kindness, anger and emotional honesty.

Carlos Castaneda.bio: Peruvian-born American anthropologist and author of The Teachings of Don Juan (1968) and a series of books about his apprenticeship with a Yaqui sorcerer. His works, hugely popular in the 1970s, remain controversial among scholars.

Henry James.bio: Henry James was an American-British author regarded as a master of literary realism and the psychological novel. His works include The Portrait of a Lady, The Turn of the Screw and The Ambassadors.

Colette.bio: Sidonie-Gabrielle Colette, known as Colette, was a French novelist celebrated for works such as Gigi and the Claudine novels. She was the first woman elected to the Académie Goncourt.

William Hazlitt.bio: William Hazlitt was an English essayist, literary critic and philosopher regarded as one of the greatest essayists in the English language. His collections, including Table-Talk and The Spirit of the Age, profiled the writers and politics of the Romantic era.

John Powell.bio: John Powell was an American Jesuit priest, psychologist and bestselling author of inspirational books on communication and self-understanding, including 'Why Am I Afraid to Tell You Who I Am?' (1969) and 'The Secret of Staying in Love' (1974).

Charles R. Swindoll.bio: Charles R. 'Chuck' Swindoll, American evangelical pastor and author. He founded the radio programme Insight for Living and served as president of Dallas Theological Seminary.

John Marshall.role: Chief Justice of the United States
John Marshall.bio: John Marshall was the fourth Chief Justice of the United States (1801-1835), the longest-serving holder of the office. His judgments, including Marbury v. Madison (1803), established the power of judicial review and strengthened the federal government.

Jane Roberts.bio: Jane Roberts was an American author and medium best known for the 'Seth' books, which she said were dictated by an energy personality named Seth. The Seth Material (1970) helped launch the New Age movement.

Norman Cousins.bio: Norman Cousins was an American political journalist and longtime editor of the Saturday Review. His book Anatomy of an Illness described recovering from a serious illness through laughter and helped popularize the mind-body connection in medicine.

Hausa.bio: A traditional proverb of the Hausa people, one of the largest ethnic groups in West Africa.

Arie de Gues.bio: Arie de Geus, Dutch business theorist who led strategic planning at Royal Dutch Shell. His book The Living Company (1997) argues that enduring companies behave like living communities.

Edwin Markham.bio: Edwin Markham was an American poet whose poem "The Man with the Hoe" (1899), inspired by Millet's painting, made him famous as a voice of labour. He later served as Poet Laureate of Oregon.

Robert Southey.bio: Robert Southey was an English poet of the Romantic school and Poet Laureate from 1813 until his death. He is remembered for poems such as 'After Blenheim' and for the first recorded version of 'The Story of the Three Bears'.

Max Planck.bio: Max Planck was a German theoretical physicist whose work on quantum theory revolutionized physics. He originated the idea that energy is emitted in discrete packets called quanta and received the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1918.

Anna Pavlova.bio: Russian prima ballerina celebrated for her ethereal style and for touring ballet to audiences around the world. Her signature role was The Dying Swan, choreographed for her by Michel Fokine.

Edith Wharton.bio: Edith Wharton was an American novelist known for depicting the upper-class society of old New York in works such as The House of Mirth. She became the first woman to win the Pulitzer Prize for Fiction, for The Age of Innocence (1920).

Edna Millay.bio: Edna St. Vincent Millay was an American poet and playwright, one of the most celebrated poets of the 1920s. She won the Pulitzer Prize for Poetry in 1923.

Cecil B. DeMille.bio: American filmmaker and Hollywood pioneer, famed for epic spectacles. He directed two versions of The Ten Commandments and won an Academy Award for The Greatest Show on Earth.

Colin Powell.bio: Colin Powell was an American statesman and four-star general who served as US Secretary of State from 2001 to 2005, the first African American to hold that office. He had earlier served as Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff during the Gulf War.

Betty Friedan.bio: American writer whose The Feminine Mystique (1963) is credited with igniting the second wave of feminism. She co-founded the National Organization for Women in 1966 and served as its first president.

Plotinus.bio: Plotinus was a Hellenistic philosopher generally regarded as the founder of Neoplatonism. His writings, collected by his student Porphyry as the Enneads, describe reality as emanating from a single source called the One.

William Lyon Phelps.bio: William Lyon Phelps was an American author, critic and scholar who taught English at Yale University for over forty years. A celebrated public lecturer and radio broadcaster on books and reading, he was one of America's best-known literary popularisers.

Nora Roberts.bio: Nora Roberts is an American author of more than 200 romance novels and the futuristic suspense series written as J. D. Robb. She was the first author inducted into the Romance Writers of America Hall of Fame.

Jules Poincare.bio: Jules Henri Poincaré was a French mathematician, theoretical physicist and philosopher of science, often described as the last universalist in mathematics. He made fundamental contributions to topology, celestial mechanics and mathematical physics.

Linda Hogan.bio: Linda Hogan is a Chickasaw poet, novelist and essayist whose works, including the novels 'Mean Spirit' (1990) and 'Solar Storms' (1995), explore Native American history, spirituality and the natural world.

May Sarton.bio: May Sarton was a Belgian-American poet, novelist and memoirist known for works such as Journal of a Solitude. Her writing explored solitude, creativity and the lives of women.

Rachel Carson.bio: Rachel Carson was an American marine biologist and conservationist whose book Silent Spring (1962) exposed the dangers of synthetic pesticides and is credited with advancing the modern environmental movement.

Hannah Senesh.bio: Hannah Senesh (Szenes) was a Hungarian Jewish poet who emigrated to Palestine and volunteered as a British paratrooper in World War II. Captured and executed in Budapest at 23, she left behind poems including 'Eli, Eli' that made her a national heroine of Israel.

Edgar Allan Poe.bio: Edgar Allan Poe was an American writer and poet known for tales of mystery and the macabre such as "The Raven" and "The Fall of the House of Usher". He is credited with inventing the detective-fiction genre.

Ben Sweetland.bio: American self-help author best known for I Will, a mid-20th-century classic on developing willpower and achieving success.

John Updike.bio: John Updike was an American novelist, poet and critic best known for the 'Rabbit' novels chronicling postwar American life. He won Pulitzer Prizes for Fiction for 'Rabbit Is Rich' and 'Rabbit at Rest'.

Carl Sagan.bio: American astronomer and beloved science communicator. His television series Cosmos (1980) and books such as Pale Blue Dot brought astronomy to a worldwide audience.

Elizabeth Montagu.bio: Elizabeth Montagu was a British social reformer, patron of the arts and a leading figure of the Bluestocking circle of intellectual women. She was also a wealthy coal owner who used her fortune for philanthropy.

Rabbi Hillel.bio: Hillel the Elder was a Jewish religious leader and sage of the 1st century BC who helped develop the Mishnah and Talmud. He is famous for summarizing the Torah as: 'What is hateful to you, do not do to your fellow.'

Alexis Carrel.bio: French surgeon and biologist who won the 1912 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for his work on vascular suturing and organ transplantation. He later wrote the bestseller Man, the Unknown (1935).

Agatha Christie.bio: English crime writer and the best-selling fiction author of all time. She created the detectives Hercule Poirot and Miss Marple, and wrote The Mousetrap, the world's longest-running play.

Dale Earnhardt.bio: Dale Earnhardt was an American NASCAR driver who won seven Winston Cup championships and 76 races. Nicknamed "The Intimidator", he died in a crash on the final lap of the 2001 Daytona 500.

Robert C. Solomon.bio: Robert C. Solomon was an American philosopher at the University of Texas at Austin who wrote influential works on existentialism, Nietzsche and the philosophy of emotions, including The Passions.

Sam Rayburn.bio: Sam Rayburn was an American politician from Texas who served as Speaker of the U.S. House of Representatives for 17 years, longer than anyone else. He was a mentor to Lyndon B. Johnson and a dominant figure in Congress for decades.

Margaret Fuller.bio: Margaret Fuller was an American journalist, critic and women's rights advocate whose 'Woman in the Nineteenth Century' (1845) is a foundational work of American feminism. She was the first editor of the Transcendentalist journal The Dial and died in a shipwreck off New York at the age of forty.

Will Rogers.bio: Will Rogers was an American stage and film star, vaudeville performer and newspaper columnist beloved for his folksy humour and social commentary. His rope tricks and the line 'I never met a man I didn't like' made him one of America's most popular entertainers.

Lee Womack.bio: Lee Ann Womack is an American country music singer best known for her 2000 hit 'I Hope You Dance', which won a Grammy Award. Her albums blend traditional country with contemporary production.

William Menninger.bio: William Menninger was an American psychiatrist who, with his father and brother Karl, built the Menninger Clinic in Topeka, Kansas, into a leading psychiatric centre. As the Army's chief of psychiatry during the Second World War, he transformed military mental-health care.

Jane Addams.bio: Jane Addams was an American settlement activist and reformer who co-founded Hull House in Chicago, a model for community social work. She became the first American woman to receive the Nobel Peace Prize, in 1931.

Eddie Cantor.bio: Eddie Cantor was an American comedian, singer and actor, a star of vaudeville, Broadway, radio and early film, famous for songs such as "Makin' Whoopee".

Francoise de Motteville.bio: Françoise de Motteville was a French memoirist whose Memoirs of Anne of Austria offer a close account of the court of Louis XIII and the Fronde. She was a lady-in-waiting and confidante of Anne of Austria.

Jim Bishop.bio: Jim Bishop was an American journalist and author whose narrative nonfiction, including The Day Lincoln Was Shot (1955), sold millions of copies. He also wrote a widely syndicated newspaper column for decades.

Thomas Kempis.bio: Thomas à Kempis was a German-Dutch canon regular best known as the author of The Imitation of Christ, one of the most widely read Christian devotional books ever written. He spent most of his life in the Mount St Agnes monastery near Zwolle in the Netherlands.

Christian Bovee.bio: Christian Nestell Bovee was an American author and lawyer known for his epigrammatic writings. His collections of aphorisms were widely quoted in the nineteenth century.

Mary Pickford.bio: Mary Pickford was a Canadian-American actress known as 'America's Sweetheart' during the silent film era. She co-founded United Artists in 1919 and was a founding member of the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences.

Doris Day.bio: Doris Day was an American actress and singer, one of the biggest film stars of the 1950s and 1960s in films such as Pillow Talk. In later life she became a prominent animal-welfare activist.

Richard Needham.bio: Richard J. Needham was a Canadian humour columnist for The Globe and Mail, known for his witty, curmudgeonly observations of everyday life. He won the Stephen Leacock Award for Humour.

Harriet Woods.bio: Harriet Woods was an American politician who served as lieutenant governor of Missouri from 1985 to 1989, the first woman elected to statewide office there. She later led the National Women's Political Caucus.

Philip Sidney.bio: Sir Philip Sidney was an English poet, courtier and soldier of the Elizabethan era. He wrote the sonnet sequence Astrophil and Stella and the prose romance Arcadia, and died of wounds received at the Battle of Zutphen.

Anne Bradstreet.bio: English-born colonial American poet and the first writer from Britain's North American colonies to be published. Her collection The Tenth Muse Lately Sprung Up in America appeared in 1650.

Marianne Williamson.bio: Marianne Williamson is an American author and spiritual teacher whose 'A Return to Love' (1992), based on A Course in Miracles, became a bestseller. She founded the meal-delivery charity Project Angel Food and has twice run for the Democratic presidential nomination.

Benjamin Haydon.bio: Benjamin Robert Haydon, English painter known for monumental historical canvases such as Christ's Entry into Jerusalem. His candid autobiography and journals are a vivid record of Romantic-era art and literature.

Ella Wilcox.bio: Ella Wheeler Wilcox was an American poet whose verse appeared in newspapers across the country. Her best-known lines, "Laugh, and the world laughs with you; weep, and you weep alone", come from the poem "Solitude" (1883).

John Junor.bio: Sir John Junor was a British journalist best known as the long-serving editor of the Sunday Express from 1954 to 1986. His plain-spoken columns made him one of Britain's most recognisable newspaper voices.

Barbara De Angelis.bio: American relationship consultant and bestselling author. Her books, including Real Moments (1994) and How to Make Love All the Time, focus on love, intimacy and personal fulfilment.

Lazarus Long.bio: Lazarus Long is a fictional character created by science fiction author Robert A. Heinlein, appearing in novels including 'Methuselah's Children' and 'Time Enough for Love' (1973), where his collected maxims appear as 'The Notebooks of Lazarus Long'.

Theodore H. White.bio: Theodore H. White was an American political journalist and historian best known for The Making of the President 1960, which won the Pulitzer Prize and transformed coverage of election campaigns. He began his career reporting from wartime China.

Melody Beattie.bio: Melody Beattie is an American author best known for Codependent No More (1986), a landmark self-help book on codependency and recovery.

Harold Nicolson.bio: Sir Harold Nicolson was a British diplomat, historian, diarist and politician, married to the writer Vita Sackville-West. His diaries and biographies are regarded as classics of the genre.

Rodin.bio: Auguste Rodin was a French sculptor regarded as the founder of modern sculpture. His works, including The Thinker and The Kiss, combined realistic detail with powerful emotion and were initially controversial for departing from academic tradition.
